cn_5184e16b1f1449a0db09.statement: -y\prime\prime+\varepsilon t^2y=\lambda(\varepsilon)y,\quad y(0)=y(1)=0.\textnormal{Let the eigenvalue branch satisfy }\lambda(0)=\pi^{2}\textnormal{. Find }\lambda\prime(0).
steps: \textnormal{At zero perturbation choose }y_0(t)=\sin(\pi t).\textnormal{Differentiate the equation with respect to the parameter and multiply by the unperturbed eigenfunction.}

cn_78d02b16e5cbbbd9303d.statement: y\prime\prime+c y\prime+2y(1-y)(y-\frac{1}{3})=0.\textnormal{Find the unique real c for which there is a strictly decreasing classical solution with }\lim_{t\to-\infty}(y,y\prime)=(1,0),\quad\lim_{t\to\infty}(y,y\prime)=(0,0).
steps: \textnormal{A candidate monotone profile is }y(t)=\frac1{1+e^{1t}},\quad y\prime=-1y(1-y).\textnormal{Substitution gives the displayed speed.}
\textnormal{To see uniqueness, write any decreasing front as }p(u)=-y\prime>0,\quad u=y\in(0,1).\textnormal{Then }p\frac{\mathrm dp}{\mathrm du}=cp-2u(1-u)(u-\frac{1}{3}).

\textnormal{The positive slope of p near zero increases strictly with c, whereas the positive coefficient of p near one decreases strictly with c. Thus if a larger speed had a second front, its p-graph would begin above the first and end below it.}

\textnormal{At any intersection of two positive phase graphs, their derivative difference equals their speed difference. A larger-speed graph therefore cannot cross from above to below. This contradiction proves uniqueness.}

cn_b266d4c3b3b2895afa77.statement: m(t)=\min_{x,y\in\mathbb R}\left\{- t \left(2 x + y\right) + \frac{x^{4}}{4} + \frac{3 x^{2}}{2} + x y + \frac{y^{4}}{4} + y^{2}\right\}.\textnormal{Find }m^{(4)}(0).
steps: \textnormal{The quadratic matrix }A=\left[\begin{matrix}3 & 1\\1 & 2\end{matrix}\right]\textnormal{ is positive definite. The quartic terms are convex and coercive, so the global minimizer is unique. Its stationarity equation is }Az+z^{\circ3}=t v,\quad v=\left[\begin{matrix}2\\1\end{matrix}\right].
\textnormal{The implicit function theorem and odd symmetry give }z(t)=t w+t^3r+O(t^5),\quad w=A^{-1}v=\left[\begin{matrix}\frac{3}{5}\\\frac{1}{5}\end{matrix}\right],\quad r=-A^{-1}w^{\circ3}.
\textnormal{The envelope identity is }m\prime(t)=-v^{\mathsf T}z(t).\textnormal{Since A is symmetric, }-v^{\mathsf T}r=w^{\mathsf T}w^{\circ3}=w_1^4+w_2^4.
\textnormal{Integrate the cubic coefficient of the derivative, or differentiate it three times, to obtain }m^{(4)}(0)=6(w_1^4+w_2^4).

cn_2c108579c68cef9aad0b.statement: \textnormal{Let rho range over probability densities on the real plane with mean zero, finite entropy integral, and covariance matrix }\Sigma=\left[\begin{matrix}2 & 1\\1 & 2\end{matrix}\right].\textnormal{Find the minimum of }\iint_{\mathbb R^2}\rho(x,y)\ln\rho(x,y)\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy,\textnormal{using the convention that zero times its logarithm is zero.}
steps: \textnormal{Let g be the centered Gaussian with the specified covariance: }g(X)=\frac{\exp(-X^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}X/2)}{2\pi\sqrt{\det\Sigma}}.

\textnormal{Thus the integral of rho times ln g is fixed, equal to }-\ln(2\pi)-\frac12\ln\det\Sigma-1.\textnormal{The Gaussian attains this lower bound, and the strict equality condition makes it the unique minimizer up to null sets.}
